content:
# Sirach Chapter 7 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Chapter:** Sirach 7 (36 verses)
**Agents:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Total Disagreements:** 20

---

## Disagreement 001 — v.3: "harvest it sevenfold" vs. "harvest them sevenfold"

**EMET:** "lest you harvest it sevenfold"
**LOGOS:** "lest you reap them sevenfold"
**PNEUMA:** "the harvest you reap will be seven times worse"
**Issue:** Greek heptaplasion autēn = "sevenfold it (fem. = injustice)." EMET is more precise — the object is "it" (injustice). LOGOS uses "them." Consensus: "lest you reap it sevenfold."

---

## Disagreement 002 — v.4: "preeminence" vs. "a place of prominence"

**EMET:** "Do not seek from the Lord preeminence"
**LOGOS:** "Do not seek from the Lord a place of prominence"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't go to the Lord looking for special status"
**Issue:** Greek prōteion = "first place/preeminence." EMET is most literal. LOGOS "place of prominence" is slightly expanded. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 003 — v.6: "break down iniquity" vs. "deal with injustice"

**EMET:** "the strength to break down iniquity"
**LOGOS:** "the strength to deal with injustice"
**PNEUMA:** "the backbone to confront injustice"
**Issue:** Greek kataneuein adikian = "to break down/overcome injustice." EMET's "break down" is literal. Consensus: "the strength to break down iniquity."

---

## Disagreement 004 — v.7: "assembled city" vs. "assembly of your city"

**EMET:** "Do not sin against the assembled city"
**LOGOS:** "Do not sin against the assembly of your city"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't do things that shame you before your whole city"
**Issue:** Greek mē hamartānes eis plēthos poleōs = "do not sin against the multitude of the city." LOGOS is clearest. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 005 — v.8: "do not repeat yourself in your words" vs. "do not give yourself over to repeating a sin"

**EMET:** "Do not repeat yourself in your words, and do not let yourself be impelled to double talk"
**LOGOS:** "Do not give yourself over to repeating a sin"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't let yourself repeat a sin — even doing it once has its consequences"
**Issue:** The Greek here is textually complex. One tradition reads "do not repeat a sin twice" (mē deuterōsēs logon en proseuchē sou); another reads "do not repeat yourself in speech." LOGOS/PNEUMA follow the "sin" tradition; EMET the "words" tradition. Consensus: LOGOS — the parallel with the following verses about moral behavior supports "sin."

---

## Disagreement 006 — v.9: "consider the multitude of my gifts" vs. "notice the many gifts I bring"

**EMET:** "He will consider the multitude of my gifts"
**LOGOS:** "He will notice the many gifts I bring"
**PNEUMA:** "God will notice all these gifts"
**Issue:** Greek blepsei eis plēthos dōrōn mou = "he will look at the multitude of my gifts." EMET is most literal. Consensus: "He will notice the multitude of my gifts."

---

## Disagreement 007 — v.10: "faint of heart in your prayer" vs. "halfhearted in your prayer"

**EMET:** "Do not be faint of heart in your prayer"
**LOGOS:** "Do not be halfhearted in your prayer"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't pray half-heartedly"
**Issue:** Greek bradynēs en proseuchē sou = "do not be slow/lazy in your prayer." "Faint of heart" (EMET) is evocative; "halfhearted" (LOGOS) captures the sense better. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 008 — v.11: "ridicule" vs. "mock"

**EMET:** "Do not ridicule a man who is in bitterness of soul"
**LOGOS:** "Do not mock a person who is bitter in spirit"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't make fun of someone whose heart is breaking"
**Issue:** Greek mē katagelās = "do not mock/ridicule." Both "ridicule" and "mock" are accurate. PNEUMA's "whose heart is breaking" overstates "bitter in spirit." Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 009 — v.13: "refuse to tell any kind of lie" vs. "do not utter any form of lie"

**EMET:** "Refuse to tell any kind of lie"
**LOGOS:** "Refuse to utter any form of lie"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't lie — ever"
**Issue:** Greek pān pseudos = "every/any lie." PNEUMA's "ever" captures the absoluteness. EMET and LOGOS are nearly identical. Consensus: "Refuse to tell any kind of lie."

---

## Disagreement 010 — v.14: "babble in the assembly" vs. "speak at length in the assembly"

**EMET:** "Do not babble in the assembly of the elders"
**LOGOS:** "Do not talk too much in the assembly of the elders"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't talk too much in the company of the elders"
**Issue:** Greek mē adoleschēsēs = "do not babble/prattle." EMET "babble" is literal. Consensus: "Do not babble in the assembly of the elders."

---

## Disagreement 011 — v.15: "laborious work" vs. "hard work"

**EMET:** "Do not hate laborious work"
**LOGOS:** "Do not shirk hard work"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't despise hard work"
**Issue:** Greek mē misēsēs = "do not hate." EMET preserves "hate." LOGOS and PNEUMA soften to "shirk/despise." Consensus: EMET — "hate" is the actual verb.

---

## Disagreement 012 — v.17: "punishment of the ungodly is fire and worms"

**EMET:** "the punishment of the ungodly is fire and worms"
**LOGOS:** "the punishment of the ungodly is fire and worms"
**PNEUMA:** "The fate that awaits the ungodly is fire and worms"
**Issue:** All three agree on content. Minor: "punishment" vs. "fate." Consensus: "the punishment of the ungodly is fire and worms."

---

## Disagreement 013 — v.18: "gold of Ophir" — all agree

**EMET:** "the gold of Ophir"
**LOGOS:** "the gold of Ophir"
**PNEUMA:** "gold"
**Issue:** PNEUMA drops "Ophir." The Greek has chrysou Ophaz (= Ophir/Uphaz, a proverbial source of pure gold). Ophir should be retained as it is Ben Sira's specific term. Consensus: "the gold of Ophir."

---

## Disagreement 014 — v.19: "sensible and good-natured" vs. "sensible and good"

**EMET:** "a wife who is sensible and good-natured"
**LOGOS:** "a wife who is sensible and good"
**PNEUMA:** "a wife who is wise and kind"
**Issue:** Greek syneti kai agathē = "sensible/prudent and good." All three are close. "Good-natured" (EMET) is interpretive; "good" (LOGOS) is more literal. Consensus: "sensible and good."

---

## Disagreement 015 — v.21: "dear to you as yourself" vs. "as you would a close friend"

**EMET:** "Let a wise servant be dear to you as yourself"
**LOGOS:** "Treat a wise servant as you would a close friend"
**PNEUMA:** "Treat a capable servant like a close friend"
**Issue:** Greek hōs psychēn sou agapēse = "love like your own soul." "Dear to you as yourself" (EMET) is more literal. Consensus: "Love a wise servant as you love yourself."

---

## Disagreement 016 — v.23: "bend their necks from their youth" vs. "train them from an early age"

**EMET:** "bend their necks from their youth"
**LOGOS:** "train them from an early age"
**PNEUMA:** "Start shaping their character from the time they are young"
**Issue:** Greek kampsōn ton trachēlon autōn ek neotētos = "bend their neck from youth." The image is yoking — like training a young animal. EMET preserves the agricultural metaphor. Consensus: "bend their necks while they are young."

---

## Disagreement 017 — v.24: "keep their bodies" vs. "guard their purity"

**EMET:** "keep their bodies"
**LOGOS:** "guard their purity"
**PNEUMA:** "keep watch over them"
**Issue:** Greek tērēson tēn sarka autōn = "guard their flesh/bodies." EMET is most literal. LOGOS interprets as "purity." Consensus: "keep their bodies" — the literal image is appropriate and Ben Sira means physical safety and chastity together.

---

## Disagreement 018 — v.26: "one whom you hate" vs. "one you have come to resent"

**EMET:** "do not trust yourself to one whom you hate"
**LOGOS:** "do not trust yourself to a woman you resent"
**PNEUMA:** "one you've come to resent"
**Issue:** Greek mē epitrepsēs autē = "do not hand over authority to her." And the following: "but if you hate her" (misousēs). LOGOS/PNEUMA soften "hate." Consensus: "do not trust yourself to one you have come to hate."

---

## Disagreement 019 — v.27: "birth pangs of your mother" vs. "mother's labor in bringing you to birth"

**EMET:** "do not forget the birth pangs of your mother"
**LOGOS:** "do not forget your mother's labor in bringing you to birth"
**PNEUMA:** "don't forget how much your mother suffered to bring you into the world"
**Issue:** Greek ōdinōn mētros sou = "the birth pangs of your mother." EMET is most literal and most vivid. Consensus: "do not forget your mother's birth pangs."

---

## Disagreement 020 — v.36: "remember your end" vs. "keep your last end in mind"

**EMET:** "remember your end"
**LOGOS:** "keep your last end in mind"
**PNEUMA:** "keep the end of your life in view"
**Issue:** Greek ta eschata sou = "your last things/end." EMET's "remember your end" is most concise and resonant. This is a memento mori. Consensus: "remember your last end."

---
